previousRecord.title: How we built the MAAT Admin Agent for gym owners
previousRecord.author: Bernat Sampera
previousRecord.description: How the MAAT Admin Agent reads the backend API through MCP-style actions, uses Jev for decisions before the AI model answers, shows widgets in the chat, runs a bench, and maps owner intents from real conversations.
previousRecord.content:
![A tiny robot at a gym front desk pulls a binder labelled Actions from a tall wall of binders labelled Actions, Decisions, Widgets, Bench and Intents, while a gym owner asks who came to class yesterday](https://samperalabs.com/images/how-we-built-the-maat-admin-agent-00-cover-efb012af5f15.png)

MAAT makes software for combat sports gyms. Since September 2026 we build the MAAT Admin Agent: a chat inside the MAAT Admin Dashboard where a gym owner asks questions about the gym in plain language. Examples: "How many members are past due?" and "Which classes were the most popular this year?" Without the agent, an owner finds these answers by hand, one dashboard screen after another.

I drive the Admin Agent project at MAAT, and I own its AI infrastructure and backend work. This article shows how we built the agent, part by part:

1. How the agent gets data from the MAAT backend API through MCP-style actions.
2. How a small Decision model, Jev, prepares each turn before the AI model writes the answer.
3. How the agent shows widgets, such as tables and charts, inside its answers.
4. How we test the agent with a bench of fixed cases.
5. How we find what owners ask for in real conversations that the agent has.

The agent is read only. Today we test it on a seeded gym and with internal users. A closed beta with customer gyms comes next.

## Using MCP-style actions to access the MAAT backend API

The agent never reads the database. It calls the same backend API that the MAAT Admin Dashboard uses, with the owner's own session. The backend stays the only authority on data and access.

![A two-tone print of a robot at a library card catalog with drawers labelled members and attendance, and a padlocked drawer labelled writes with a sign Not until phase 3](https://samperalabs.com/images/how-we-built-the-maat-admin-agent-02-actions-3da68e1ea340.png)

The agent reads an action card before it calls the API. The write drawer stays locked until a later phase.

### One action for each read route and fixed parameters

The MAAT backend publishes a typed contract for its routes. The agent has an action registry on top of that contract. An action has a name, a domain, a description for the model, an input schema and a handler. The handler calls exactly one read route. Some routes give several actions with fixed parameters. For example, the backend's attendance insights routes give 15 attendance actions, such as a check-in count, the most popular classes and the peak hours. Today the registry has 2 member actions and 15 attendance actions.

Each action lives in its own file inside its domain folder:

```text
src/core/domains/
  members/
    domain.ts
    actions/
      list.ts
      detail.ts
  attendance/
    domain.ts
    period.ts
    actions/
      count.ts
      top-classes.ts
      peak-hours.ts
      by-weekday.ts
      ... 15 actions in total
```

The input schema reuses the contract schema, so the model cannot send a field that the API does not accept. We write every description by hand. A description says what the action reads and names its result fields.

### How the model discovers actions with `list_domains`, `list_actions`, and `run_action`

The model does not see every action at the start. It sees three tools, in the style of an MCP server:

1. `list_domains` returns the domain names, with one line for each.
2. `list_actions(domain)` returns the actions of one domain, with descriptions and input schemas.
3. `run_action(action, input)` checks the input against the contract schema, calls the route and returns the result.

We took this router pattern from an earlier MCP proof of concept at MAAT. Today the agent calls the registry in its own process, not through an MCP server. The registry does not depend on a transport, so a real MCP server for external hosts can wrap it later.

### How the user's token and the gym scope reach each API call

The dashboard sends the owner's Firebase ID token and the gym slug with each message. The agent checks the token and asks the backend which gyms the user can access. A chat is bound to one user and one gym when it starts.

The handler sets the gym slug from the chat. The model never sees the slug as an input, so it cannot ask about another gym. The token goes with every API call, and the agent never stores it. The backend route guards then decide what each staff role can see.

Errors come back to the model as a short closed list of codes, such as `ACCESS_DENIED`, `DATA_UNAVAILABLE`, `NOT_FOUND`, `INVALID_INPUT` and `ACTION_FAILED`. An expired session ends the turn.

### How a test keeps the action registry read only

The backend contract also has routes that change data. A forwarded token could call them. The registry is the control.

A test reads the contract metadata of every registered action and checks that its route is a GET. The test has a negative case: it registers a real write route, `members.setCashMembership`, and expects a failure. If someone adds a write action by mistake, the build fails. Writes come in a later phase, with owner approval for each change.

## How we use Jev as a Decision model before the AI model writes the answer

Each owner turn has two kinds of model calls. We gave them names so that the team uses the same words.

![A two-panel comic. A small referee named Jev reads the owner's question and fills a clipboard with Scope yes, Effort low, Language English, Domain members. Then Jev hands the clipboard to a large writer named AI, who says Thanks. I skip the guessing](https://samperalabs.com/images/how-we-built-the-maat-admin-agent-03-decision-generation-382f062e79b0.png)

Jev reads the question first and fills in the plan. The AI model writes the answer from that plan.

### The difference between the Decision call and the Generation call

The **Decision call** is one small, fast request at the start of each turn. Today the Decision model is Jev. Jev does not write text. It returns a probability for each question that we ask about the owner's message.

The **Generation call** writes the answer and calls the tools. A larger AI model does this work, through OpenRouter. In this article, "the AI model" means this Generation model.

In the code, the two parts live in separate folders. One object, the `GenerationPlan`, is the only bridge between them. The Decision code asks the questions and applies the thresholds. The Generation code reads only the plan.

```ts
// Simplified from src/core/decision/plan.ts
interface GenerationPlan {
  answerMode: Decided<'answer' | 'decline'>
  thinkingEffort: Decided<'low' | 'high'>
  language: Decided<AnswerLanguage | undefined>
  domain: Decided<string | undefined>
}
```

### The four questions that Jev answers for each message

All questions go to Jev in the same request. Code turns the probabilities into the plan:

| Plan field | Question to Jev | Rule in code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answer mode | Is this message about the gym? | 0.5 or more: answer. Below 0.5: decline politely. |
| Thinking effort | Does the message need careful multi-step thinking? | 0.5 or more: high reasoning effort. Otherwise low. |
| Language | Is the message written in English? In Spanish? One question for each of 9 languages. | Exactly one language at 0.7 or more: the AI model gets a fixed line with the answer language. Otherwise the AI model decides. |
| Domain | Which domain holds the data? One multiple-choice question. | The domain with the highest probability. The AI model gets its action list. |

The language check has one yes or no question for each supported language: English, Spanish, Catalan, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch and Polish. A name, a number or a very short message does not establish a language. In that case no language passes, and the AI model decides.

Jev has 2 seconds. If the call fails, the plan uses safe defaults: answer the question, low effort, no language line and no preloaded domain.

Two days of hourly probes on production gave a typical Jev time of 0.22 seconds, and 0.27 seconds at the 90th percentile. This is short compared with a full turn.

### How the wording of a Decision question changes the result

The text of each Decision question matters as much as the threshold. An owner typed "¿quién vino a clase ayer?" ("who came to class yesterday?") as the first message of a chat. Jev scored it 0.21 for scope, and the agent declined. The scope question described the gym in general words, so "class" and "who came" looked like a general request.

We did not change the model. We added one paragraph to the scope question. It says that the gym is a combat sports studio where members attend classes, check in, pay memberships and book. The same message then scored 0.93.

![Dot plot of Decision model scope scores. Before the change the lowest attendance score was 0.08 and the example question scored 0.21. After the change the lowest attendance score was 0.80 and the example scored 0.93. Off-topic questions stayed at a highest score of 0.06](https://samperalabs.com/images/how-we-built-the-maat-admin-agent-01-scope-score-d216f04ddfa2.png)

The added gym vocabulary moved all 16 attendance test questions above the pass line. Off-topic questions stayed low. One run per variant.

### How Jev selects the data domain and preloads its actions

The domain question sends Jev the description of each domain, such as members or attendance. The domain with the highest probability goes into the plan. The AI model then gets that domain's action list in its prompt, so it can call `run_action` at once, without the discovery steps. All three router tools stay available. If the preloaded actions cannot answer the question the AI model looks in another domain before it declines.

Our first design asked one yes or no question for each domain. Jev scored both domains above 0.5 for every test message, so it never picked one. One multiple-choice question picked the correct domain for 5 of 5 test messages.

### Why a separate Decision model reduces steps and cost

We could ask the AI model to make these decisions itself. But each decision then costs a full model step, and the model can forget a rule in a long prompt. Jev answers narrow questions fast, and code applies the thresholds. The decisions are numbers that we can trace, test and change.

The domain choice shows the gain. Before we made it the default, we compared it on the bench with 70 test turns:

| Measure | Without domain choice | With domain choice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model steps | 213 | 121 |
| `list_actions` calls | 48 | 1 |
| Input tokens | 609k | 485k |
| Cost | $0.047 | $0.029 |

Model steps fell by 43%, input tokens fell by 20%, and cost fell by 39%.

## How widgets are defined, loaded, and rendered in the chat

Some answers are better as a table or a chart than as text. We call these components widgets. The AI model chooses the widget itself, after it has the data. Jev has no part in this choice.

![Annotated mockup of a chat answer. The owner asks which members are past due. A run_action members.list call comes first, then a members table with three fictional members and their status, then one short sentence. Four numbered notes explain the definitions, the data call, the show_widget call and the short sentence](https://samperalabs.com/images/how-we-built-the-maat-admin-agent-04-widget-anatomy-77b749fc873f.png)

The widget comes first, then at most one short sentence. Simplified illustration with fictional members.

### The 16 widgets of the MAAT dashboard chat

At MAAT we built 16 widgets for the dashboard chat:

- **Tables**: `MembersTable` for a list of members and `BreakdownTable` for a ranking, such as the most popular classes.
- **Values and cards**: `StatValue` for one number, `MemberCard` for one member, `CoachCard` for one coach, and cards for a class, a coupon, a product and a schedule.
- **Drafts**: `EmailDraft` and `DocumentDraft`. The owner copies the text. The agent does not send email.
- **Charts**: `ColumnChart`, `AreaChart`, `StackedBarChart`, `DonutChart` and `Heatmap` for attendance series and breakdowns.

The class, coupon, product and schedule cards wait for their read actions. Their definitions tell the AI model not to show them yet.

### How the dashboard sends widget definitions with each message

The agent does not store the widget list. The dashboard sends all widget definitions with each message. MAAT can add or change a widget in the dashboard without a change to the agent.

A definition tells the AI model when the widget fits and what it needs:

```json
{
  "name": "MembersTable",
  "description": "Shows a table of gym members. Use for member names and membership statuses. Do not use for empty results or other records.",
  "useWhen": "Default for a members.list result with two or more members. Not for one member, a count or an empty result.",
  "needsData": true,
  "params": {},
  "rows": {
    "name": "Member first name as text.",
    "lastName": "Member last name as text.",
    "membershipStatus": "Membership status as text."
  }
}
```

`useWhen` says when the widget fits. `needsData` says that the widget shows values from an API result. `params`, `optionalParams` and `rows` name the fields.

### How the AI model picks a widget from a one-line catalog

The agent turns the definitions into a compact catalog in the system prompt, with one line for each widget: the name, when it fits, and its fields. A short rule comes with the catalog:

- When a widget fits the result, call `show_widget` first, before any text. Then write at most one short sentence.
- A widget that is the default for a result fits that result. The owner does not need to ask for a widget.
- Show only values from a tool result of this turn, or the text of a draft that you write.
- Never show a widget when the owner asks for text only.

The order "widget first" is important. One provider dropped a `show_widget` call that came after text in the same step. In a replay test, 8 of 10 such calls were lost. With the widget call first, 12 of 12 calls arrived.

### How the server validates the call and the dashboard renders it

The `show_widget` tool has one input schema for each widget. The server checks the values against the schema of the selected widget. It also accepts small format differences, such as a number in place of text.

Two guards protect the answer:

- **No data, no widget.** If a widget needs data and the turn has no successful `run_action` call, the server refuses the call. The AI model then calls the action first, or answers in text.
- **Lost widget calls.** Sometimes the model spends the tokens of a widget call, but no call arrives. The agent detects this and runs one more step with the tools off. In that step the AI model writes the data as a short list or a table, so the owner still sees one complete answer.

The client gets each shown widget as `{ shown, widget, values }`. The dashboard maps it to a widget part at the same position in the message. Streaming and page reload use the normal message path.

## How we benchmark the agent with fixed cases on a seeded gym

A prompt change can fix one answer and break another. We do not trust a change until the bench agrees.

![Scatter plot of four screened models by mean full turn time and passed turns out of 11. Mercury 2.5 and our current model passed 10, Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite and Command A Plus passed 8](https://samperalabs.com/images/how-we-built-the-maat-admin-agent-05-model-screening-efd2a0ee4cd0.png)

Four models from a 20-model screening. One run per case, so this is a screening, not a calibrated accuracy measure.

### Writing the ten owner questions before the agent code

Before the first line of agent code, we wrote ten owner questions. Seven were about members, such as the member count, payment problems and recent joiners. Three were about attendance. Each question had the correct answer on a seeded gym, the expected API calls and a pass rule. Seven refusal cases followed. Examples: a question about another gym, and a member name that contains a hidden instruction.

These questions chose the first API routes. Four read routes answered all ten. They also became the first test set.

### The core tier of 10 cases and the full tier of 66 cases

The bench now has 66 cases. It runs the agent core without the chat platform, against a seeded development gym, through the real development API. A seed check confirms the facts in the gym data before we trust a score. Jev scores each answer against the expected answer.

The cases have two tiers:

- **Core** has 10 cases. It runs after a prompt, action or tool change. It covers member filters, a list followed by a detail lookup, follow-up turns, attendance statistics, Spanish, injected names, an unsupported request, a request for the system instructions, and an attached file.
- **Full** has all 66 cases. It runs before an important release or after a large change, such as a new model.

Widgets have their own bench. It has 42 cases and uses a copy of the 16 widget definitions from the dashboard. A sync check compares this copy with the dashboard.

### Comparing 20 models on accuracy, speed, and cost

The model is one line of configuration, so the bench can compare models. We screened 20 candidates on two cases. Then we ran the best candidates on 10 cases, for 11 turns each, and compared accuracy, time and cost.

We kept our current model for the internal test round. It passed 10 of 11 turns, and it was already live. Its full run passed 18 of 23 turns, at about $0.0009 per turn. The launch model is still an open decision.

### Limits of the judge score, and why we read failures by hand

An automatic judge makes mistakes in both directions. In one run, an answer passed with a score of 0.57, but it gave the wrong start date for the period. Two other answers were correct, but the judge failed them.

So we read every failure. One failure taught us an important rule. An owner asked about invoices, and no action reads invoices. The agent did not decline. It got the list of unpaid members and gave it as a substitute. The data was real, but it answered a different question. We added a rule: decline unavailable data, and offer no substitute until the owner asks. After three prompt rounds, the targeted cases passed 11 of 12 attempts.

## How we capture owner intent from real conversations

The bench tests the questions that we expect. Intent analysis shows the questions that owners actually ask. It reads real conversations that the agent has, and it tells us which owner goals the agent answers well, which it answers badly, and which it cannot answer yet.

![The intent map as rows of marks, one row for each of 15 domains and one mark for each intent: 54 read, 72 change and 8 help intents. Members has the most intents with 25, then subscriptions with 22 and payments with 15](https://samperalabs.com/images/how-we-built-the-maat-admin-agent-06-intent-map-eaa89f411c59.png)

The intent map lists the goals that an owner can have. An intent in the map does not mean that the agent can do it.

### Step 1: collect conversations and split them into owner goals

Every agent turn sends a trace to PostHog, our analytics tool. The intent analysis downloads selected conversations from these traces.

One conversation can contain several requests. A preparation step uses Claude to split each conversation into separate owner goals. It also completes short follow-ups. For example, "and last month?" becomes a complete question with its subject. Code then attaches the original question and the agent's answer to each goal, with no changes.

### Step 2: match each goal to the intent map with Jev

The intent map defines 134 owner goals, called intents, in 15 product domains. Examples of domains are members, payments, schedule and bookings. Each intent has a kind:

- **Read**: the owner wants information, such as a check-in count.
- **Change**: the owner wants to change data, such as a member's plan.
- **Help**: the owner asks how to do something.

More than half of the intents, 72 of 134, change data. The agent is read only today, so these intents show the size of the work for the write phase.

Jev matches each goal in two steps. First, it scores the goal against each domain. Then it scores the goal against the intents of the selected domains. The scores decide what happens next:

| Score | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 0.8 or more | The intent is proposed as a match. |
| 0.2 to 0.8 | A person reviews the match. |
| Below 0.2 | The intent does not match. |

Nothing is forced. A goal can match several intents, or none. A goal with no match can show that the map needs a new intent.

### Step 3: check the answers and plan the next actions

A separate step checks whether each answer appears to meet its goal. A local website, Intent Explorer, shows the results by environment, gym and intent. It has a list of **unmet requests**: goals that the agent answered only in part, or not at all.

Each request moves through a small queue: Inbox, Investigating, Resolved or Archived. One button copies an investigation prompt for a coding agent, with the evidence attached. The unmet requests then tell us which actions, widgets and Decision questions to build next.

## What we learned while building the agent

These points apply to any agent that answers questions from business data:

1. **Write the questions before the code.** Ten questions with known answers chose our routes, our first actions and our first test set.
2. **Use the API that your product already uses.** The agent reuses the backend contract, the user's session and the route guards. It needs no separate access rules.
3. **Put the rules where code can check them.** A test keeps the registry read only. Code applies the Decision thresholds. The backend computes every total.
4. **Give narrow decisions to a small model.** A fast scoring model decides scope, effort, language and domain. The large model writes the answer and chooses the widget after it has the data.
5. **Read real conversations, not only test results.** The bench checks known questions. Intent analysis finds the questions that you did not expect.
